    {
      "startEvent": 140,
      "endEvent": 148,
      "contextStartEvent": 117,
      "contextEndEvent": 157,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "and not really interested in finding out the truth about reality.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["shame"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Denial of the causal premise itself licenses an accusation of truth-indifference (E140–148), discounting the skeptic without addressing the objection's merits. This protects an explicitly intuitive premise rather than supplying a standalone slogan. Craig distinguishes his original presentation from subsequent supporting arguments (E149–157) and later substantively engages Malpass's objections."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 544,
      "endEvent": 560,
      "contextStartEvent": 487,
      "contextEndEvent": 600,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "being only comes from being",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After Malpass asks why uncaused beginnings are impossible (E535–543), the maxim restates the causal restriction rather than independently establishing it. However, Craig explicitly identifies a metaphysical intuition, previously offers a discrimination argument (E306–340), and next disputes the substance distinction (E565–600). Whether this use replaces reasons or summarizes that position remains uncertain."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 683,
      "endEvent": 695,
      "contextStartEvent": 660,
      "contextEndEvent": 695,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "physicists therefore have nothing to tell us about the reality of the soul.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The categorical dismissal could exclude relevant physical evidence about minds, but its immediate support is expressly conditional: if mind-body dualism holds, the soul is not material (E687–695). The passage does not clearly reject empirical objections to dualism itself. It is therefore uncertain whether this establishes protection beyond a disputed disciplinary boundary."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1040,
      "endEvent": 1041,
      "contextStartEvent": 992,
      "contextEndEvent": 1153,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Well, then he needs to reform his intuition.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["shame"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Asked what happens when a reader lacks the intuition, Craig makes that disagreement a reason to correct the reader (E1038–1041), without establishing why his intuition takes priority. This locally protects the argument, although it is not a general affirmative slogan. His subsequent response offers historical examples and a consistency rationale (E1103–1153)."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1617,
      "endEvent": 1655,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "I can get to the end of the beginningless.",
      "explanation": "The memorable formulation summarizes an explicit asymmetry: an endless ascending count lacks a final number, while the proposed beginningless countdown has an endpoint. Malpass limits the conclusion to a gap in the symmetry argument, rather than claiming to have established the countdown's possibility."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2186,
      "endEvent": 2212,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "I don't claim that you can show that the creator of the universe is omnipotent",
      "explanation": "Craig expressly limits the conclusion, declines commitment to Scotus's stronger argument, and explains his weaker power inference through creation without pre-existing material. The inference remains disputed, but its stated rationale and qualifications make this an informative non-slogan argument."
    }
